ERWIN SINGER RECEIVED HIS CERTIFICATE in psychoanalysis from the William Alanson White Institute in January 1956. He became a faculty member in 1958, a training and supervisory analyst and Fellow in 1968. He served the Fellows well as a member of the Nominating Committee. He leaves behind a legacy of admired writings, enriched students, enhanced analysands, and grateful colleagues.

My first contact with Erwin was in 1967. He, Bernie Kalinkowitz, and I spent time together discussing the desirability and feasibility of a university affiliation for the Institute. Erwin's intelligence, candor, and humor were apparent in these discussions. This was the beginning of a number of conversations between us about various Institute matters. I found him generous with time, ideas, and money. He introduced a number of his friends to the Institute; they have since become generous supporters.

PASCAL SAID: "LE SILENCE ÉTERNEL DES ces espaces infinis m'effraye." Such is the existential anguish, the Angst, which accompanies human life, created by the experience of the world as uncanny and by the knowledge that this experience must be confronted. What helps to overcome the uncanny? The great religions offer refuge from the overpowering through belief in God, but they also command that people Love one another. Love is the highest and most positive form of contact with the Other and thus with reality, broadening the closed (and thus isolating) circle of our daily experience. It may provide those with strong convictions and beliefs with a means of reaching outside themselves, and thus with the ability to develop a sense of the Universal.

To encounter a person fully is to be in touch with his inner-most self, his spiritual essence, in a way that is more fundamental than a rational understanding of "dynamics" and "conflicts." One may have a genuine encounter with another person and be moved deeply by it, without feeling the need—or possessing the ability—to articulate the bond in logical and consciously chosen terms. Such a contact creates the conditions for mutual understanding and a feeling of enrichment. This directly opposes the isolation and alienation of the self-absorbed person who can see the world only in relation to narrow, personal goals and concerns.

The infant develops the ability to make nonverbal contact with the Other in large part through emotional encounter with his parents. Participation and communication within the family at an early age imply the curiosity which helps to form an outgoing attitude rather than one of dependent expectation.

I FIRST CAME TO KNOW ERWIN SINGER while he was in training at the White Institute. We were drawn to one another. He was eager to learn and to speak up; it was a pleasure to have him in a seminar because he was bright, alive, and genuinely interested. He had a searching mind and enjoyed collaborating in a positive way. There was nothing argumentative or petty in his style. His skepticism was reassuring, never oppressive. It was a pleasure to have him in one's midst. He brought from his homeland Vienna a love of the finest in its cultural tradition; music, art and poetry were interests that were important to him and he shared those interests with anyone who cared to join him. Erwin and I truly cared for one another. There was a tested mutuality and loyalty in our friendship, our relationship became collegial as well, and it was with confidence that I referred patients to him. He did not fail to recognize the challenges of his profession with seriousness, integrity and vitality.

At one period, Erwin helped me with a personal problem. This was dealt with over a stretch of time with skill, tact and affection.

ROY SCHAFER'S (1976) CALL FOR a new language for psychoanalysis, which he has named "action language, " represents a great step forward. Aimed at the reifications, classifications and anthropomorphisms of Freud's metapsychology, action language represents a conceptualization of man as an active, unified, purposive, responsible individual.

Schafer's fundamental rule is:

We shall regard each psychological process … as some kind of activity, henceforth to be called action, and shall designate each action by an active verb … and by an adverb (or adverbial locution), when applicable, stating the mode of this action. Adopting this rule … we shall not use nouns and adjectives to refer to psychological processes. … This … is what it takes really to discontinue physicochemical and biological modes of psychological thinking (p. 9).

Woodworth's Principle

This brings back to memory a similar call nearly fifty years earlier by Robert S. Woodworth, 1869–1962, addressed to psychology in general. Woodworth was considered the dean of American psychology as professor of psychology at Columbia University where he taught for over fifty years. A profound, soft-spoken scholar, author of important books on experimental psychology, schools of psychology and dynamic psychology among others, his orientation was one of functional psychology with a psychology of motivation added. His introductory Psychology was virtually the standard text at the time, going through five editions between 1921 and 1947. "For exactly 25 years it outsold all other texts so greatly as to be beyond competition" (Boring 1950, pp. 564–565).

Reflections on the Analytic Process after Forty Years as a Psychoanalyst

Walter Bonime M.D.

Walter Bonime

Walter Bonime, M.D.
10 Park Avenue
New York, New York 10016

Walter Bonime  

IT WAS MY FORTUNE TO ENTER THE field of psychoanalysis at a time of ferment. The new and challenging ideas of Karen Horney (1937), (1939), unacceptable to the New York Psychoanalytic Institute, led to her resigning from the faculty of that organization to establish with an eclectic group of colleagues a new teaching institute. It was hoped by all, that here the spirit of exploration would replace an atmosphere of dogma. In that new institute, I was a member of the first class; and Erich Fromm (1941) was part of the first faculty.

The following remarks are not a reminiscence or critique of Fromm, nor are they a distillate of my years in our profession. They reflect, however, what continues to be professionally exciting to me on a daily basis; they reflect work in progress.

I have never "cured" anyone; I feel, however, that I have helped a number of people in their efforts to live more fulfilling lives. As I consider my therapeutic role, certain activities and related concepts come to the fore as ones I use with growing confidence.

Though I do not like, after forty years, to begin on a negative note, the above allusion to the daily excitement of our work brings to mind a contrasting problem. This is the problem of boredom, a complaint about which one hears from colleagues of all ages.

When the analyst is bored, I believe something is going wrong, something not entirely engendered by the patient. A way I've found for dealing with boredom is to question the completeness of my own involvement; the chances are that I'm not fully listening, not adequately responding. And there must be good reasons.

ERICH FROMM'S BLEND OF SCHOLARSHIP and common sense is no more in evidence than in his small volume entitled, "The Forgotten Language". In this book he took a major step toward demystifying dreams and dream work and preparing the way for their more general accessibility. Very early in the book he calls attention to an unfortunate consequence of Freud's classic contribution to our understanding of the dream:

Another limitation is that interpretation of dreams is still considered legitimate only when employed by the psychiatrist in the treatment of neurotic patients. On the contrary, I believe that symbolic language is the one foreign language that each of us must learn. Its understanding brings us in touch with one of the most significant sources of wisdom, that of the myth, and it brings us in touch with the deeper layers of our own personalities. In fact, it helps us to understand a level of experience that is specifically human because it is that level which is common to all humanity, in content as well as in style (Fromm 1951).

Not only was it necessary to clear the air, as Fromm did, of certain mistaken notions about dreams and the exclusive position held by the therapist in relation to them, but, what was also needed, was a way of implementing this point of view. Turning his attention elsewhere, Fromm never got back to this task. Freud and later, Jung had addressed the general public on the subject of dreams. Freud emphasized the unique role of the psychoanalyst. Jung went further, in efforts to orient the public to dreams, but he too felt that specialized knowledge and training was essential. In the light of the views they held neither could provide the non-professional with the tools needed to comprehend one's own dreams.

HANS STRUPP, WHO WAS TRAINED IN PSYCHOANALYSIS at the Washington School, is known for his careful and thought provoking research on what makes for negative and positive results from psychotherapeutic endeavors (Hadley and Strupp 1976), (Strupp et al 1977). This article, from an expert is another excellent contribution. There is little with which I can disagree. So my comments will be by way of emphasis, expansion and explication.

Since the basis of Strupp's discussion is a book by Dorte von Drigalski, who describes her unsatisfactory experiences with two psychoanalysts, while a candidate at a German psychoanalytic training institute. Strupp's essay is concerned therefore, with (her) training analyses.

Training is a most unfortunate adjective to apply to psychoanalytic treatment. The aim of a psychoanalysis is to help a patient overcome personality handicaps which cause suffering and which interfere with growth and development. A "training" analysis has the additional purpose of ridding an analytic candidate of blindspots which interfere with his practicing psychoanalysis and of enabling him to use himself and his technical skills in the best possible way. It has nothing to do with training as training. It is a psychoanalytic experience, a voyage of self discovery.

So I applaud Strupp when he points out that the objective of any psychotherapy, including psychoanalysis, is

to help the patient achieve what he or she is seeking. It must alleviate pain and suffering and it must result in greater self-realization and inner strength … Conversely, a therapeutic process in which such changes are conspicuously absent is cause for concern.

Approaches in Psychotherapy (A Conference)11

WITHIN THE PSYCHOANALYTIC perspective on psychotherapy evolving from Freud's pioneering insights into human suffering, many different schools of dynamic understanding and treatment approaches have emerged. These include classical, interpersonal, object relations, self-psychology, existential, and family schools, among many others. The present conference assessed the application of some of these approaches by senior psychotherapists—each within the psychoanalytic framework—to the clinical material from one patient's treatment. The source of data for clinical discussions was the work of Michael Balint, as reported in his book Focal Psychotherapy (Balint, M., Ornstein, P., and Balint, E.) (London: Tavistock Publications, 1972). Clinical discussion examined alternate views on the meaning of the clinical material and on the utilization of therapeutic technique by Dr. Balint in his treatment. Panel discussions focused on issues raised by the presentations.

MY TASK IS TO PRESENT some alternative approaches to the clinical material described by Dr. Balint. My views emerge from the perspective of a family and marital therapist.

The very honesty and completeness of Dr. Balint's report makes one feel apologetic for picking up the many transparent clues he provided which lead to alternative interpretations of the data. My own view is that Balint was so locked into his formulation by his short-term goals that he could not attend to the loss themes which were cropping up in his patient's material. Only after two futile attempts to terminate did Balint come to see significance in Baker's sense of loss and move beyond the initial formulation, namely the patient's inability to enjoy victory over adversaries. The work was then successfully concluded and a follow-up almost seven years later indicated that the improvement had been sustained.

WE NOTE IN THE REPORT OF Balint's case a variety of interventions—interpretative, empathic, manipulative, individual, familial, and various mixtures of these. Perhaps in keeping with sectarian biases, we assign importance to these interventions. For example, Malan, in his discussion of the material, emphasizes the interpretation, particularly, I think, of the oedipal material (Malan, 1963). Others emphasize the sharing of pain and aloneness, in keeping with Myerson's formulation, that "the patient was suffering from hurt and lonely feelings" (Myerson, 1977). Gustafson, in a recent, remarkable account of the material, emphasizes Balint's manipulation of the transference, his disconfirming the transference, or, to use the language Gustafson perfers, Balint's passing the patient's tests (Gustafson, 1981).

There are still other possibilities. Balint himself mentions the patient's "newly won identification with the therapist" (p. 69) and the patient's having "introjected my ideas and words" (p. 115). He does not discuss how this was achieved. One could also emphasize the building up of the patient's confidence against father's reiterative denigrations, what I call counterprojection and, in some instances, counterintrojection.

Benjamin Wolstein  

L. Chertok and R. de Saussure, The Therapeutic Revolution: From Mesmer to Freud. Translated by R. Ahrenfeldt. New York: Brunner/Mazel, 1979. 226 pages.

IT IS A SIGN OF THE SELF-CONSCIOUSLY evolving present of psychoanalysis that its serious researchers are, with increasing frequency, once again turning to a review and reconstruction of its history. In view of the current efforts to observe and define, explain and interpret such dimensions of therapeutic inquiry as the psychology of the self and the immediate psychic experience of first-personal processes, and their variants, it is, in fact, even becoming necessary to look back at that history, and to rework it from the standpoint of the new post-modern perspective.

This new therapeutic inquiry is, of course, emerging against the backdrop of the established, modern, post-Freudian perspectives. It goes directly to the dynamics of the immediate, first-personal experience of the uniquely individual self relating to the mediate, social and cultural behavior of the ego-interpersonal (or object-relational) other. It, therefore, points up the dynamic aspects of the historical development of psychoanalytic inquiry that, during the 1930s, imperceptibly faded into the shadows of that earlier post-Freudian work, as epitomized in such various modern perspectives as character analysis, ego psychology, interpersonal, and object relations.

Those 1930s approaches are, as a group, all part of the outward movement of psychoanalytic thought into the environing conditions of the patient's life.

Come then—he said—weigh me a pound of fire, measure me a bushel of wind or call back a day that has passed
The Apocrypha, Esdras, 2nd Bl. 4-5

IN HIS Rhetoric, ARISTOTLE (1927) DESCRIBES the aged: "They live by memory rather than by hope, for what is left to them of life is but little, compared to the long past." Moreover, the elderly "are continually talking of the past, because they enjoy remembering." Aristotle's description of the aged, one that emphasizes the importance of memory and the past, is not uncommon, particularly when young people perceive their elders. Do the elderly, however, perceive themselves in this fashion? Almost every old person, when asked "Do you feel old?" will respond "No, I do not feel old." This almost universal condition of not feeling old is best understood in relation to the old person's connection with his past and memory. Not feeling old, does not mean unawareness of limitations and disabilities, but is certainly related to the image that the elderly have of themselves. Because life is a process in time, with continuity as the hallmark, we arrive at old age feeling that we are the same person we used to be. The old do not feel old because they continue to see themselves as the same.

Do elderly people have a long past? What is the meaning of a long past? Does it mean a rich and extended experience that would make life more meaningful? Is the life of the elderly meaningful? Let us consider each of these questions in turn.

Long experience has been considered an important feature of the "wisdom of the aged." In primitive cultures where traditions could not be passed on in writing, old people were honored as the teachers of tradition. Experience itself was the valuable tool.

Introduction the Case of Mr. Baker

Andrew Morrison M.D.

Andrew Morrison

Andrew P. Morrison, M.D.
32 Hawthorn Street
Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138

Andrew Morrison  

THE PATIENT: Mr. Baker, a 43 year old man, married, and the father of two sons and a daughter (all in their teens), was referred to Dr. Balint in November, 1960 by the patient's concerned family doctor. A psychiatrist had previously seen the patient and had recommended hospitalization because of Mr. Baker's "increasing preoccupation with his wife's feelings towards a young man who seriously courted her before their marriage and with whom she had no further contact whatsoever." Mr. Baker experienced a "serious breakdown" about six years previously, which had gradually receded over several months.

During World War II the patient had been in Cyprus where he met his wife, a Turkish woman. They fell in love when he was 24—she was his first serious involvement, although he had several women before, mostly prostitutes. Her family opposed their relationship, because of racial and religious differences. Their sexual and emotional involvements were intense, short of intercourse, before he was sent to India. On the Burma front, he corresponded frequently with his fiancee-to-be, but after he was hospitalized for dysentery her letters stopped. He became agitated, cabled, and finally received a letter informing him that she had met a young Turkish officer (from Cyprus) and they had fallen for each other. She was uncertain as to which man to choose, and Mr. Baker wrote frequently imploring her to choose him. She wrote back that she had chosen Mr. Baker, had broken up with the other man (James), and he had departed. The couple had a happy interlude together on Cyprus until he was sent to Italy, where he remained until the end of the War. He returned to the family business, which increased to an excellent position, mainly due to his efforts. Their marriage was happy from the start, and they had three children, all, according to him, well-adjusted.

Ever since his marriage, he had wondered how his wife could have had any feelings towards James (the other man).

THE BOOK FOCAL PSYCHOTHERAPY IS a fascinating and carefully elaborated documentation of the treatment of a man in a paranoid state. The authors of the book investigated the feasibility and effectiveness of choosing and sticking to a major focus for therapy. Doctor Balint, in treating the patient, deliberately overlooked clinical material and responses of his patient that might have suggested another focus. The authors cogently present their reasons why this particular focus was selected. They indicate both the positive and negative effects that the therapist's interventions based on achieving his aim had upon the patient. In an unusually honest manner, Balint presents his own reactions and state of mind during and after the therapeutic sessions—the interpretations he considered giving but did not, his fears about treating so disturbed a person, and his confusion when he did not understand what was taking place. In chapters written after Dr. Balint's death, Dr. Ornstein thoughtfully discusses the patient's treatment experience as a process and the nature of the patient's personality and illness. He straightforwardly highlights the problems in treating someone with a major disturbance by a focal psychotherapy.

Paul Wachtel  

I WISH TO DISCUSS CERTAIN implications of a point of view I have come to call cyclical psychodynamics because it locates the heart of the psychodynamic process not in the patient's preserved past but in the vicious cycles which past events set in motion. This approach is rooted in the theoretical contributions of writers such as Horney (1939), Sullivan (1953), and Erikson (1950), but departs from their views at significant junctures and reworks them in ways they themselves might find uncongenial. The resultant has a great debt to each but makes on claim to being true to any.

Central to this point of view is the notion that the seemingly infantile wishes and ideas that are revealed in psychoanalytic work persist not in spite of the person's present reality but precisely because of it. When one looks closely enough at the person's daily interactions, one finds that each person skews his experiences in distinctive fashion, selecting with whom to interact and evoking particular sides of those he does encounter so as to make his environment as unique and pathognomonic as a fingerprint. When one looks carefully at the fine details of the patient's daily interactions, there turns out to be no "average expectable environment."

Hartmann's (1939) introduction of that term was, to be sure, part of an effort to bring reality back into psychoanalytic theory, to amplify the perspective—never fully absent from psychoanalysis but kept well in the background until the 1920's—that looked for the roots of our actions not just in drives welling up from within

Joyce McDougall  

THE LAST FIFTEEN YEARS HAVE seen considerable research devoted to the concept of narcissistic libido and the conflictual theoretical questions to which it gives rise. These issues are derived from the attempt to conceptualize the clinical problems presented by patients who show manifest disturbance in their narcissistic economy. They have also given rise to a new clinical category: the "narcissistic personality disorder". There is little doubt that our clinical confusions and theoretical dissensions are reinforced during those periods in the history and development of psychoanalytic thought where clinical observation seems to be at odds with established psychoanalytic theory, or appears to be dealing with hitherto unencountered phenomena. The abundant literature on narcissistic problems, while it reveals widely divergent interpretations of these, nevertheless concurs in giving the impression that today's analysands are of a different calibre or indeed structure than those studied in the first half century of psychoanalytic research. The patients of today, with their "psychotic parts", their "narcissistic shields", their "grandiose selves", their "operational thinking" and their "alexithymic defects", seem strangely dissimilar from the "good classical neurotics" of the Belle Epoque.

Is there, in fact, a "new" or "modern" analysand? Or indeed a new or modern narcissism? (Hanly and Masson, 1976)

Arthur Gottdiener  

PSYCHOANALYTIC STUDIES OF THE IMPOSTOR have traditionally focused on intrapsychic conflicts. The purpose of this paper is to provide an additional dimension by reviewing the literature and clinical core material from an interpersonal perspective.

Accounting for the ability of the impostor to assume a false identity, Greenacre (1958a) notes that it "… appears that the fraud was successful only because many others as well as the perpetrator had a hunger to believe in the fraud …" She then says, "To this extent those on whom the fraudulence is imposed are not only victims but unconscious conspirators." Unfortunately, this theme is never developed further, and the possibility of an interpersonal approach to this problem is subsequently ignored.

The psychoanalytic study of the impostor began in 1925 with a paper by Karl Abraham (1925) entitled, "The history of an impostor in the light of psychoanalytical knowledge." Abraham saw the patient twice, once in 1918 when he was in the army and a second time when he was a civilian five years later.

The original psychoanalytic investigation had been ordered by the presiding judge of a military court. The prisoner had been found guilty on a number of serious charges including desertion during war-time, falsely assuming higher military rank, and a number of thefts, forgeries and frauds. At the first examination Abraham had concluded that the prisoner's condition was unalterable and chronic.

Because of a general amnesty, the prisoner was released in 1918, but again arrested on some of the same kinds of charges in 1919. However, for a variety of reasons he was not imprisoned and was only brought to trial in 1923.

WHILE REREADING MY PRESENTATION AND DISCUSSION of the therapeutic process in this paper, I thought that I might have conveyed the somewhat misleading impression of having understood things earlier and more easily than was actually the case.2 During its first two years, I experienced this treatment situation, for the most part, as exceedingly dull and confusing. The experience was mitigated only by the fact of the patient's making what appeared to be good and steady therapeutic progress. I had little more in the way of understanding than the sense that in accepting things as they were I was probably meeting some basic therapeutic need in my patient. My understanding only gradually gained in clarity, aided by certain concepts from the work of Melanie Klein (1946), (1951), Racker (1968), Winnicott (1958), (1965) and Spotnitz (1969), (1976). In general, I have found these writers helpful in enabling me to make some sense of difficult treatment situations involving patients who present primitive mental states. I have for some time been assimilating certain of their contributions into the core of my psychoanalytic understanding which had been established in my training at the Wm. Alanson White Institute.

The more recent influences are perhaps more apparent in the presentation than are the earlier ones. Yet Racker did cite as one of the important factors determining the multiple technical variations and divergencies in psychoanalytic practice, "the genealogic factor, that is to say, the influence of different 'archifathers' and 'fathers' upon the technique of their analytic children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren" (Racker 1968, p. 25).

Samuel Lipton  

DEWALD UNDERTAKES TO DOCUMENT an entire analysis in considerable detail in order to present data for other analysts to study and also to inform the public of the nature of psychoanalytic material (p. 7). The patient he reports on was a 26-year-old woman who suffered from symptoms of anxiety and phobias. The analysis lasted for 347 hours over a two-year period, and as a result of it the patient was relieved of her symptoms. Dewald wrote detailed notes during the patient's sessions, and he bases his report mainly on them. Because they were so voluminous he could not publish them all but limited himself to publishing the detailed notes from 108 hours, choosing the notes of seven complete months taken from the beginning, the middle, and the end of the analysis, and summarizing the rest of the analysis. In addition, at an unspecified time after the analysis had been concluded, Dewald wrote discussions of each of the detailed reports of the 108 hours and a 42-page synthesis at the end. The book includes laudatory statements by Fleming and Anthony and Anthony's report of his interview with the patient three and a half years after the end of the analysis.

As significant and serious an effort as the book is, Dewald has gone even further than his stated goals, and in his 108 discussions and in his synthesis he has written what amounts to an abbreviated textbook of psychoanalytic theory and practice. However, he has been able to do this only by excluding all references to controversial issues, and he conveys thereby the idea that the analysis which he reports is representative.

THEORIES OF PSYCHOANALYTIC SUPERVISION appear to be in a period of renaissance. I tend to approach the topic with more or less the same combination of caution and optimism that characterizes my interest in psychoanalytic theory in general; as an intellectual adventure I relish in the same way I enjoyed taking apart clocks during preadolescence … to see how they worked. But I don't think it is at all necessary to have an explicit theory in order to work effectively. In fact, I suspect that too great a preoccupation with it can interfere with the process of supervision or therapy in the same way that taking apart clocks can become a substitute for full involvement in the business of living.

During a recent analytic session a patient said with an "Alice-In-Wonderland" delivery: "Life is a good example of what goes on in analysis." Resuming the Work with a Life-Threatening Illness

Ann-Louise Silver M.D.

Ann-Louise Silver

Ann-Louise Schlesinger Silver, M.D.
Chestnut Lodge
500 West Montgomery Avenue
Rockville, Maryland 20850

Ann-Louise Silver  

SUDDENLY, IN JULY OF 1978, I FACED a life-threatening illness requiring major surgery and prolonged debilitating treatments. My surgeon ordered me to resume work promptly, seeing anxiety and self-preoccupation as stressful. He was convinced that stress interferes with the immune system, this the mysterious but decisive factor in survival. He viewed work as a life-saving distraction. Thus, I was transformed from an ebullient junior colleague to a fatigued, pale, despondent individual as I fought to keep my spirits above the waters of self-absorbed despair. If the ideal therapist serves as a secure container for the projected affects of the patient, I guiltily thought of myself as more a collander or saturated sponge than a container. So, I returned to work at Chestnut Lodge, partly as a therapist, partly as a patient on an occupational therapy assignment. My patients became part of my metaphoric treatment team, giving to this work their best and very effective efforts, replete with the expected ambivalences. It was as if they too had been drafted to fight at the front lines of a confrontation with death. I wish to convey, through a series of vignettes, something about this phase of the work, and then to offer a few comments.

Initially, the staff tried to spare my patients the news, but it became clear some patients already knew. For example, among my initial visitors to the hospital was an intrusive 26-year-old borderline woman who had left the Lodge a few months earlier against medical advice. She appeared at the hospital soon after I'd left the intensive care unit. So, the six administrators of my six patients met with each of them, informing them of the situation as they each understood it. Interim therapists were assigned.

Introduction

Freud's Use of "Object"

OBJECT RELATIONS THEORY HAS GRADUALLY become such an expanding and so broadly inclusive a term that it is in need of redefinition. The term "object" was first used by Freud (1905) when he referred to the agent either upon which (whom) the instinctual drives were discharged and/or the agent which (who) facilitated the discharge. He first posited a stage of libidinal development known as autoerotism which was objectless. The autoerotism of the libidinal zones were later to be organized first under the authority of the narcissistic organization in which the ego was taken as the id's first libidinal choice via the autoerotic zones, and then under the Oedipus complex where the autoerotic zones had finally become more fully organized and directed to an object beyond the ego. His first use of object then was as an external person who had something to do with gratifying the instinctual drive and/or in helping the infant and child to repress it. Phantasies about these objects were not considered internal at this time. Freud used the term "father complex" to denote the importance of this external presence. The "mother complex" was not to be formulated until many years later by analysts other than Freud.

Freud counterposed a stage of development between autoerotism and anaclitic object choice which he called narcissism, a stage which was both primary and/or secondary.

PSYCHOANALYSTS CAN BE ROUGHLY DIVIDED into two categories: those who believe that the essence of psychoanalysis is the detoxification of fantasy and those who believe that the essence is the demystification of experience. Dr. Dewald is clearly of the first persuasion and I, as will become evident, am of the second, so some difference of opinion is inevitable. The first category, detoxification of fantasy, requires that the therapist believe that people are made ill by their fantasies, by the symbolic distortions of a reality which is either innocuous or, even when deleterious, no more than a trigger for the fantasy systems which are energy-driven (libido) and universal—that is, built into the deep structure of people. So everyone has an Oedipus complex with its primal fantasies. The function of the therapist is to permit a controlled regression so that the patient comes into conscious touch with the primary process fantasies. Daylight chases away the bogey-man.

Not to enlighten one who can be enlightened is to waste a man; to endeavor to enlighten one who cannot be enlightened is to waste words. The intelligent man wastes neither his man nor his words. — Confucius

Man is a mystery. One must solve it. If you spend your entire life trying to puzzle it out, then do not say that you have wasted your time. I occupy myself with this mystery because I want to be a man. — Dostoevsky2

THESE TWO SEEMINGLY CONTRADICTORY statements summarize the dilemma and my attitude towards the issues of reanalysis as well as to analysis in general. Confucius speaks of waste of time, in our frame of reference referring to analyzability, or treatability, while Dostoevsky alludes to the endlessness of the process of self-investigation. And yet, these statements are complementary.

This paper is based on 53 cases of reanalysis from my practice. Selection was guided by the elimination of patients analyzed by inexperienced therapists in order to avoid the use of candidates or supervisees as guinea pigs. I confined myself to patients who had been engaged for two to seven years in analysis with experienced, even outstanding analysts, recognized as experts in the field.

That is, in terms of difficult patients, we ought to know who's being difficult with whom, under what conditions, in what way, and to what ends. Recently there has been a surfeit of panel discussions and symposia on the difficult, the borderline, the narcissistically oriented, or those with primitive mental states. One wonders whether this is a new syndrome which we have just recently discovered, or whether it's all a healthy attempt on our part to extend, quite legitimately, our area of influence, and to come to terms with working with those patients who present themselves for help, but who do not seem to conform to a set of rules which some people hold dear.

As a matter of fact we might ask the question, do the difficulties reside in the patient or in the analyst, or better, in the interaction to which both contribute and for which both are responsible?

Perhaps it isn't the word "difficult" which we ought to consider but the word "the." Since as soon as we hear the attribution "the" attached to any appellation, diagnostic category, or social group, we are listening to a reification.

Gladys Natchez  

ERWIN SINGER WAS A MULTIDIMENSIONAL man. He was an actor, ski instructor, photographer, xray technician, a gourmet, restauranteur and sommelier, investor, art collector and fighter for political freedom. Those who knew him were touched by his vitality, his depth, his charisma, his lustiness, gusto, fullness and love of life. They also knew his skill as a psychoanalyst, supervisor, professor and author.

He was born in Vienna, and Vienna was part of the fiber of his existence. He visited that city every two years and never gave up yearning to go back "home" to live permanently.

European culture also was a major influence on him. All his life he expanded his knowledge of philosophy, art and religion. He believed strongly in Talmudic and biblical values, and during these last years had been thinking of writing a book which he had tentatively entitled "Visions and Values." He believed that a psychoanalysis which encompassed only academic psychological concepts was lacking in scope so he brought his varied experience, background and education into all his relationships.

He always aspired toward independence of thought and action yet was quick to add that to be independent one had to recognize the inevitability of one's dependence.

His writings stressed the importance of separating oneself and developing "the frightening sense of individuality, the terror of freedom and the horror of responsibility" (1978). He thought that "the evolution of a. … unique and separate identity rather than the achievement of strong identification aids humans in their fight for fulfillment" (1965). He believed that many of us make desperate attempts to maintain some sense of identification because we cannot conceive of separateness within human solidarity (1965, p. 171). Writing of the terror of separateness he used the example of a man who stands up among others, particularly among those he respects (or from whom he wants approval) and takes an iconoclastic stand; it is a frightening place to be.

THE INTERNATIONAL UNIVERSITY MENÉNDEZ PELAYO has honored its invited guests from Spain and other countries by encouraging expressions of homage to Erich Fromm. Via the presentation of papers, the initiation of seminars and discussion groups, it is the wish and hope of all of us that we can perpetuate our affection, respect for, and gratitude to Dr. Fromm.

Fromm's faith in man and in man's possibilities for growth persevered throughout his life. His concern with the human condition in its most immediate and also its broadest sense emerged while he was still a young man. This attitude toward himself and toward others would seem to have had its origins in a dedication to grasp the nature of love. To have known Fromm and his writings, I believe, lends support to this assertion. The love for man, and for his fate, have been of signal importance for Fromm. This is attested to in all his contributions. Clarifications in the search for the understanding of love have been central in his works: vide "The Art of Loving"; but more to the point, the theme of love has flowed into the crevices of all of his inquiries. To him, the concern with love was never the exclusive province of the arts, literature, or the church; loving must be an activity lived out by man as part of his responsibility to himself and to his fellows.

Marianne Eckardt  

"HE [FROMM] LIVES IN A day when the sun has gone out of the human condition, and all his writing starts from the conviction that the life of Western man has gone desperately wrong. This sense of urgency which pervades Fromm's work has made of it an ambitious system of social criticism … But if Fromm's criticism runs deep, it is because his hopes run high. He thinks that man today has everything within his grasp—if he will reach out for it. In this, too, Fromm seems a man of the twentieth century, which has not known where to draw the bounds of human life" (Schaar 1961).

It is true that Fromm hoped; but it is not true that his hopes ran high, nor that he believed everything is within man's grasp. Unfortunately, Schaar failed to comprehend the essence of Fromm's theme of hope. The quality of hope was centrally important to Fromm, and he attempted to describe it with great care. An understanding of his meaning of hope is essential also to an understanding of his style of writing.

I will first comment on his style of writing and then highlight his ideas about what hope is, about hope as an essential quality of the structure of aliveness, about shattered hope, and about the vital relationship between suffering and hope.

Fromm wrote most often in the spirit of the prophet mode. Central to the prophet's message is messianic hope or messianic vision. This messianic vision rests upon the tension between what existed and what was becoming, was yet to be. This vision, or that which is hoped for, may not be realized in one's lifetime, yet one must expect the messiah every day. Hope is thus paradoxical. It is neither passive waiting, nor is it an unrealistic forcing of circumstances that cannot occur.

IN RECENT YEARS, PSYCHOANALYSTS have begun to examine the specific structure of the supervisory situation and its techniques. The present paper is an attempt to explore a particular dimension of supervision seldom examined in specific fashion: the supervisory crisis. Because of the wide scope of this important topic, the present contribution will focus on a single aspect of this situation: the use of dreams spontaneously reported by supervisees to their supervisors as a means of conceptualizing and dealing with supervisory crisis situations.

It is to be stressed at the outset that the present study does not imply that supervisors should request from their supervisees the report of dreams or other personal communications. To the contrary, the model of supervision that provides the framework for the present study is focused on process note presentations from supervisees and the unconscious supervisory efforts of his or her patients. Instead, this presentation is based on a supervisory finding that on rare occasions supervisees spontaneously report dreams to their supervisors. Quite often, this occurs at a time of supervisory crisis, when a supervisee is under severe stress from one or all of the following factors: (1) A personal crisis in his or her therapeutic work and more rarely in his or her outside life; (2) an especially troublesome and highly specialized problem with the patient under supervision; (3) a special and highly disturbing difficulty with the supervisor to whom the dream is reported.

BEGINNING WITH THALES IN THE 6th century B.C., the pre-Socratic Greek philosophers took a tremendous step forward from the chaotic and unpredictable theology of Homer and Hesiod (Chessick 1977). For the philosophers, the cosmic processes were not personified but rather conceived of impersonally and with emphasis on natural and necessary movements. They did not repeat ancient doctrine but instead reached their own conclusions, made of sweeping generalizations, often not carefully reasoned. Above all, they introduced the Greek notion of a well ordered harmony in the universe, a kósmos, the first principles of which were thought to exist externally.

With the questions of whether there is anything orderly in, or anything that serves as the ground of the apparent world of chaotic appearances, we have the beginning of metaphysics. Metaphysics does not possess a method to reach truth either analogous to or the same as the method of experimental science, which has proven so powerful and efficient in our time toward the advancement of empirical knowledge of the universe. Indeed, we know that the answers to the crucial questions that all metaphysics ask cannot be found by the methods of experimental science.

William James (1890) said, "Metaphysics means nothing but an unusually obstinate effort to think clearly." As Socrates explains in Plato's Theatetus(1937): "We no longer seek for knowledge in perception at all, but in that other process, however called, in which the mind is alone and engaged with being." For the man of action involved in the world of everyday life, the questions metaphysics asks are profitless. THERE IS A TRADITION OF EXCEPTIONAL difficulty in the psychoanalysis or other psychotherapy of depressives. Edith Jacobson (1954) spoke of a more intensive affective involvement with them. She referred to intervening with a "spontaneous gesture of kindness or even a brief expression of anger, " but wisely added, "… since these patients are frequently very provocative and exasperating, such a deliberate show of emotional responses naturally presupposes the most careful self-scrutiny and self-control in the analyst." Sullivan (1954) commented on the depressive's functioning as particularly difficult to comprehend and deal with, the person "remaining, " as he expressed it, "most remarkably obscure and unknown." Freud (1959) found in the depressive "an attitude of revolt, " which is a formidable barrier to productive therapeutic collaboration. Frieda Fromm-Reichmann (1959) noted the depressive's "lack of interpersonal sensitivity, " which we can recognize as an emphatic hindrance in exploring interpersonal experience; she may also have been referring to a quality in the depressive which Freud (1959) characterized as "incapable of love." Despite the distinguished status of the analysts here referred to, and many more could be quoted to confirm the arduousness of working with depressed people, I feel safe in suggesting, as the most impactful single reference to cite, one's own personal professional experience.

This sketchily indicates a consensus regarding an inherent difficulty in psychotherapeutic approaches to the depression prone person.

Introduction

LISTENING TO A PATIENT HAS BECOME immensely more complicated and controversial since the days of Freud. His original conception was that the therapist listened with "free floating attention" and attempted to attune himself like a receiver to the transmitting unconscious of the patient as it revealed itself through derivatives in the free associations (Freud, 1962). As these derivatives or disguised presentations of the patient's unconscious conflicts and wishes presented themselves in dreams, transference material, and free associations, the therapist gradually formed hypotheses about the patient's unconscious thoughts and presented these back to the patient. This is a fairly clear-cut and time tested procedure, requiring the proper training on the part of the therapist and above all a minimum of countertransference interference with the therapist's capacity to assess the patient's data and to formulate meaningful and well timed interpretations and communicate them to the patient (Chessick, 1969), (1971), (1974), (1977a), (1977b), (1980a).

There are since Freud's time a number of extremely important additional and complementary conceptualizations which greatly help us in the understanding of patient material. All of these are controversial and in some of their theoretical preconceptions they contradict each other. However, they are quite useful in lending additional perspective to the patient's data and in helping us to form additional hypotheses about where the patient is at. Most of these assume that therapists are well trained and free of serious countertransference difficulties; that therapists are not suffering from a "core psychosis"; and that they are capable of making interventions which are not primarily a manifestation of their own needs.

I AM GREATLY HONORED TO HAVE been invited to talk about Erwin Singer's contributions to psychoanalysis. I had, of course, over the years read his papers, his book and book chapters, always impressed by his cogency and amused and touched by his loyalty to his friends. Erwin hardly ever wrote a paper without a series of laudatory references to his friends' publications. I owe to Erwin the heady, and, alas, never-to-be-recaptured, experience of finding myself in reference as, "as Freud, Jung, Fromm and Levenson have said…"

Over the years, we talked often about theoretical and clinical considerations, and, particularly in the early years, when the White Institute maintained a Summer Palace at Provincetown, Erwin, Ed Tauber, Ben Wolstein and I spent many pleasant afternoons up to our ears in sand and stimulating ideas. It was a time of heady rebellion and strong personalities, and Erwin with his Viennese flamboyance and diaspora-inspired background often seemed to me more the contemporary of my mentors than of my own somewhat more colorless, managerial generation. Nevertheless, we became fast friends and stayed friends over a thirty-year period. Time and familiarity breed a certain… nonchalance, and it was only when I was able to review Erwin's total oeuvre, that I realized how coherent and vital his work was, how sympathetic to my own perspectives, and how vividly it reflected his personality and style.

If a leopard wrote metapsychology, it would be about spots, and when Erwin wrote, it was about the impact of the therapist and his personality on the treatment.

IT IS COMMONLY HELD THAT THE creation of technical language is the necessary means to the understanding of new truths; this is easily demonstrated in the physical sciences. Atomic physicists theorized that atomic particles consist of more elements than they had previously imagined, so they were forced to give names to these entities. Proton and electron were not enough. Now they imagine quarks, mesons and muons. Testing these ideas experimentally they found them useful in predicting atomic phenomena. Indeed, they could not proceed without the invention of the new vocabulary. Other sciences have developed and grown similarly. Their growth can be charted by the development of their technical languages. Psychoanalysis has likewise evolved and continues with a technical language which is purported to reveal truths about human behavior hitherto unknown. Robert Coles, in discussing the philosopher-novelist, Walker Percy and his (Percy's) attitude toward scientific method and human relations says:

One makes hypotheses, comes up with inductions or deductions. One does tests in order to verify. One shows oneself able to predict. All very well, when it is the physical world of the life cycle of plants and animals that is under scrutiny. Let man himself be the subject of research and we have what is sometimes called the 'human sciences' and certain notorious difficulties.

We psychoanalysts have flooded the language with "oedipus complex, " "transference, " "resistance, " "defense mechanisms, " "cathexis, " "projective identification, " "splitting, " Ad infinitum and thereby proclaim that with these "instruments" we have plumbed new depths into the human psyche. We have what Stephen Jay Gould has called a case of "physics envy".
